toc.title: Why shutdown can feel like home
What coming out of shutdown can bring up
Small moments go a long way
Not your fault, but your responsibility
The sun is above the clouds
They showed up with what they had

blocks.p: If you're stuck in dorsal vagal shutdown, you probably need to hear a little positivity and encouragement, and not just from me, but from other people who know what you're going through.

A while back I ran a Shutdown Experiences Survey. People shared what shutdown is like for them and how it affects their daily life, their thoughts, their emotions, their relationships. At the end I asked two more questions: Is there anything else about your experience you want to share? And if you could share a message with someone else experiencing shutdown, what would you say?
This is what they said, to you, the reader who's in shutdown too, along with my thoughts on it.

The morning I recorded this, it was foggy and a little rainy. Still a little dark, very overcast, with a chill in the air I could feel on my skin. I had my beanie on and my sweater on. To me, that's perfect shutdown weather. It tells us: go indoors and be warm. Maybe have a loved one there, but being alone is okay too.

We'll start with a touch of humor. One person, who's been in shutdown for eleven to twenty years, wrote simply, "Hang in there," with a picture of a sloth hanging from a branch. If you're in shutdown, you'll get it.
One listener wrote:

q: I think the feeling of shame over being shut down is one of the biggest issues for me. I now understand what's going on, but I've been so ashamed for so very long. Ashamed for not being able to perform at the level that I knew I was capable. For being constantly late for everything. For not being able to do more to make others happy. And the list goes on.

blocks.p: I think that's probably common. Shame goes hand in hand with shutdown, or pretty much any stuck defensive state. People tell you you're not good enough, you're not doing enough. And part of you might agree: "I know I'm capable of doing more, so maybe I'm not doing enough." And then, "Maybe I'm not good enough."

Let's remind ourselves that what you accomplish is an aspect of who you are, but it's not all of who you are. Being in shutdown is an aspect of who you are, your present autonomic state. It's very dominant right now, but there is more to you. Maybe it's not coming out because the shutdown is so prevalent. Hopefully, over time, especially as you practice safety, the shutdown eases. For now, it's a good idea to remind yourself that there is more to you, and it will come out as the shutdown eases.
The same listener had this to say to you:

q: Shutdown is nothing to be ashamed of. It's how your body is protecting you. It's actually a gift, even though it rarely feels that way. When you learn to work with it, it can be your guide to a richer and more fulfilling life.

blocks.p: Even though she carries a lot of shame about her shutdown, she recognizes that being in shutdown is not, in and of itself, something to be ashamed of. I completely agree. It's simply a state of the body, an autonomic state. We're not in it randomly. We're in it because of the context of our life, past or present. There's something we don't feel safe in, can't run away from, and can't fight off, so the last option, the last one in the sequence, is to shut down. The body collapses. It goes numb. We disconnect. It's an evolutionary survival strategy. Not something we like or choose. It's just the body's last option for dealing with whatever it's dealing with.
In that context, there's nothing to be ashamed of. There's a reason. It makes sense. "My autonomic state is normal, based on the context of my life."
If you can validate your shutdown, just acknowledge it, and then normalize it, that's a really good sign. The next step is: can you give yourself permission to be in shutdown?
Another listener put it this way:

q: Shutdown can feel like forever. Calm and grounded can seem so impossible that it isn't even on the map to get out of shutdown. But it's there. Your body and mind want to help you. You're in shutdown because a part of you is trying to protect you. Honor that part. It wants to help. It just doesn't know how.

blocks.p: I love this. Can you acknowledge what you're feeling? Can you normalize it, that it's there for a reason and maybe even protective? And can you give it permission to be there? Even though it seems so far away, it is possible to reach safety. It's possible to have small moments of calm, relaxation, or connection. Basically, stillness. Stillness is your safety state combined with your shutdown state. Can you be in shutdown and have your safety state active too? Yes, it's very much possible. And step one might be just reducing the stimulation around you.
Another wrote, "Your body is telling you to lower your stimulation. Listen and get soothed. You are worth it."
And another:

q: I would like you to become conscious of this state of yours and accept it. There were things in life that moved you down the Polyvagal ladder. Be self compassionate. There is nothing wrong with shutting down. It's your system signaling you that "I can't take anymore."

blocks.p: I completely agree. The only thing I'd tweak is the word "accept." The way I read it, that doesn't mean you have to be okay with it. Accept means validate it, recognize it, normalize it (that it's not random, it's there for a reason, it's your body saying "I can't take any more"), and even give it permission to be.

So what does giving yourself permission to be in shutdown look like? Can you give yourself permission to reduce stimulation? Maybe be alone? Turn the lights down? Bundle up in warmth? Can you give yourself permission to be in silence? That's how you work with it. You listen to what your body needs, and you provide it.

Isolating in the dark and cutting people out of your life is not exactly what I mean. Isolation is different from solitude. In shutdown, solitude is probably a really good idea. Isolation, probably not. Can you give yourself at least moments of solitude where you feel what you feel? You don't distract yourself with TikTok and Instagram and YouTube videos. You truly let yourself feel shut down, and then allow your body to self-regulate out of it. Not easy, but that's the general idea. That's how you settle into stillness. A cold, foggy, overcast day is a really good day, if you're in shutdown, to embrace solitude and warmth and less stimulation while you watch the rain outside.

blocks.h: Why shutdown can feel like home

blocks.p: One listener shared this:

q: I don't think I'd call it insight, but recently I've noticed that I can quite strongly long for a shutdown state, especially when I'm in a freeze state, but also when I'm in flight fight. They stretch me out so much that I crave the numbness and disconnection of shutdown somehow. I'm not quite sure how this works within me, but I can imagine that more people, especially with trauma, feel this craving toward the shutdown state sometimes.

blocks.p: I think you're right. Whatever stuck autonomic state we have, even a defensive one, becomes predictable. Not really comforting, but predictable. We know what to expect. There are no surprises. As we self-regulate out of it, things are suddenly different. We come out of shutdown, which is disconnected and slow and alone, into flight or fight, and suddenly there's a surge of fight activation. We feel more aggressive, irritable, angry. That's different. It feels wrong. It feels like we're doing something wrong, like there's something wrong with us. "I'm not a person who does this. I'm not a person who thinks this way."

But the reality is that you're a person with the potential to think this way and that way, and to feel this way and that way. As we self-regulate out of any stuck state, it feels different, and different isn't necessarily welcome. We get comfort and predictability from what we know, so we might want to go back there, even though we know it's not ideal.
She added this for you:

q: Try to identify what shutdown feels like and looks like for you, and then allow yourself to give into the shutdown tendencies instead of fighting it because it's not what you're supposed to feel or act like. For me, at least allowing myself to be in shutdown has opened a door to gently ease out of shutdown toward a safety state instead of getting stuck in fight, flight, or freeze.

blocks.p: Instead of fighting it because it's not how you're supposed to be, embrace it. Shutdown has a function. It evolved in us for a reason. Does it limit your capacity to work and kick butt in life, and to connect with others and build meaningful relationships? Yes. It's limiting, just like fight and flight and freeze. But it's not bad. There's no one way you're supposed to think and act and feel.

So can you give yourself moments of calm, relaxation, and stillness? Can you get in that warm blanket with a warm tea, versus telling yourself "I'm not supposed to feel like this" and distracting yourself with your phone? Can you be with one person who feels safe, who you smile with and who accepts you fully, versus isolating in your room with the lights off, watching a whole series in one day? In each pair, one is more embracing of shutdown than the other. Instead of fighting it, can you connect with it compassionately on some level? That completely depends on the strength of your safety state.

blocks.h: What coming out of shutdown can bring up

blocks.p: Another listener wrote:

q: I'd be interested to know more about the different degrees of shutdown because I'm convinced there is a mild form that all of us are in a lot of the time, but we're still functional and able to do stuff. We're just not connected to our bodies or the here and now. One particular challenge for me is that I can see how shutdown protects me from certain aspects of my life that are too painful to deal with like chronic fatigue and isolation. Coming out of shutdown means being more aware of those things, and I can't change those things, especially isolation, unless I come out of shutdown. It can't change overnight and it's not easy to change. So there's this bit in between where I'm super aware of my dissatisfaction with my life and I can see why my nervous system goes into shutdown to cope with this reality.

blocks.p: I definitely agree with the first part. I think each of us has some disconnection, maybe some shutdown, present within us every day. All these states are on at all times, really. How many of us are aware that we have emotions in our body? There's a chronic, top-down disconnection we all have, from family, culture, political and social stuff, our interpersonal issues, our own internal issues where we reject how we think and feel. All of it together: disconnection, disconnection, disconnection. That's probably a daily, chronic, underlying shutdown we all have, though disconnection can come from flight and fight as well.

And yes, shutdown has a function. Some things in life are too much, and shutdown helps numb us from the pain of them, like a chronic illness. That doesn't change overnight. As we come out of shutdown, we become more aware of how unhappy we are with life. We were probably aware of it in shutdown too, but coming out, we have more fight activation, so the frustration with life and how we're functioning in it probably goes up.

That's potentially a really good sign that you're coming out of shutdown. If you're not as numb, you're not as shut down. It might come through as irritability, aggressiveness, or anxiousness. If you're feeling those things, hey, you're not as shut down as you were before. Can we embrace those feelings and keep climbing the [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system)? It's possible. And again, the strength of your safety state is incredibly important: mindfulness, maybe meditation, maybe using movement to channel that activation.
One listener described what that climb was like:

q: All I say to people in shutdown is that shutdown sucks. And it does get so, so, so much better. There is more to life than what you in shutdown have been experiencing. I spent 28 to 29 years being disconnected, dissociated slash in shutdown. And I can personally say through my experience that going from shutdown to experiencing safety is very difficult. And for me, it is not fun. And it is filled with steps backwards and weird curves on the road to recovery. But even though it is the most difficult thing I have ever and will ever experience, I would encourage every person who is stuck in shutdown to just keep trying. Keep moving through life, because getting out of shutdown is 100 percent worth it: experiencing safety and experiencing connection with people. Oh my gosh, I can't even come up with the words to describe how magnificent these things are. Work through shutdown at your own pace, but you can do it. It is possible, and it is worth it.

blocks.p: I'd definitely take that advice. She's not saying it's a magic pill, or that a hack or some vagus nerve stimulation will fix you overnight. It's a process: slow results from small efforts. That's a lot better than nothing, and it's pretty normal.

blocks.h: Small moments go a long way

blocks.p: The listener who wrote about degrees of shutdown said this to you:

q: If you're experiencing shutdown right now, please know that you haven't failed. You're not broken. You're just overwhelmed and your nervous system is trying to cope with that in what it thinks is the best way. Be gentle with yourself. Maybe you can do one small thing that brings you some comfort or brings a tiny bit of awareness to your body.

blocks.p: I love that idea of one small thing. I think it's huge. In my community, I do daily challenges, and a lot of the time it's just: what's one small thing you can do now? What's one two-minute mindfulness exercise you can do now? Those little micro moments of safety, of mindfulness, where we connect with what we're feeling inside, are enormous, and can do a ton in shutdown, especially because in shutdown things seem so overwhelming. A two-minute mindfulness exercise, or even a thirty-second one, is probably a lot better than a thirty-minute meditation you're struggling through. Seriously.
Others said the same thing in their own words:

q: This too shall pass. Put one foot in front of the other and allow yourself to make small shifts, small wins, no judgment, only compassionate inquiry. Gradually things will change.

You're not alone. There is help out there and finally there is light at the end of the tunnel. The Polyvagal Theory has been the life saving rescue for me. I've actually had glimpses of being able to think clearly and not being afraid. Soon I hope the glimpses will come together more and I can live peacefully and enjoy my life and not be afraid anymore. Just try it because it brings tremendous relief even with only the small glimpses at first. But you will feel yourself trying to come alive and that causes you to keep trying to get into ventral vagal safety to finally start feeling free of the drudge, confusion, and fear you feel now.

blocks.p: Those small moments go a long way. Don't give up. Do the small moments.
One more:

q: Someone once told me, when you're going through hell, keep going. Movement's important even if it is a cup of water to your lips and bread to your mouth.

blocks.p: This is so good. Why stay in hell? Make at least small steps forward, and those small steps might be drinking a little water, eating a little bread, just taking care of the basic foundational pieces. Your hand to your mouth doesn't seem like much, and I guess it's not, but it's better than lying in bed oversleeping. It's better than swiping your thumb on your phone hour after hour. A small movement might even be sitting quietly for two minutes, using your eyes to reorient to the environment, seeing where your eyes take you. It's a tiny movement, just your eyes, but you're reconnecting to the environment. I think that's better than lying in bed in the dark, shaming yourself.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.h: Not your fault, but your responsibility

blocks.p: One person, who has been in shutdown for more than fifty years, wrote simply, elegantly, and poignantly: "This is not your fault."

I agree. But I'll add something. You might blame yourself. "All I did was stay in bed all day. I didn't live up to what I want to be as a parent, or an employee, or a business owner. Maybe this is my fault. I'm choosing this state every day. I'm choosing my thoughts."

It's completely okay to take stock, to audit your daily life and look at what you are and aren't happy with, what you're not proud of. Nothing wrong with that at all. Now, is your stuck shutdown state your fault? The reason it's there, probably not. But can you take responsibility, every day, for doing something differently? I think that's a really good idea. Even though it's not your fault, the responsibility is on all of us to self-regulate out of our stuck defensive states. Hopefully we help each other and have co-regulators in our lives, but ultimately, it's up to us.

So while it's probably not your fault that you're stuck in shutdown, it is your responsibility, and there are things you can do every day to feel a little more proud of yourself. Instead of binge watching a show, can you do a two-minute meditation or mindfulness practice? Can you reduce stimulation for two minutes, exist in silence, give yourself permission to feel what you feel, and maybe say something kind to yourself? You can probably do that.

None of us is going to fully self-regulate out of shutdown, completely and forever, starting now. But we can absolutely take steps in that direction every single day. In this moment, right now, you have an opportunity to do that, and I really hope you embrace it, so you end your day with less regret, guilt, and shame, because you did something different.
One listener shared a really descriptive experience of shutdown, and why so few people understand it:

q: How rare it is for anybody to know about it. You can't tell most people, "Oh, I'm in shutdown right now."

blocks.p: She described a group mushroom ceremony where she cried for most of three hours. "That level of crying is dysregulating for me. It was not cathartic in that context." The guide wouldn't acknowledge that she'd had a hard time and kept pushing her to see the positive. "I told her that I was in shutdown and was unable to find the positive or feel it. She just kept pushing and pushing." She got to the point of telling the guide she wanted to be downstairs under her bed. "I described shutdown repeatedly, thinking she'd eventually get it, but she never did. She was obsessed with how I needed to drop my limiting beliefs, and I'd be fine."

q: I hope you can see the shutdown in the story. It shows up and most people don't know what they are seeing, and yet I'm pretty sure everyone in that ceremony has been in shutdown. They just didn't know it, and perhaps they don't get stuck. And healing professionals who think they know healing, well, in my view, they all need Polyvagal Theory training.

blocks.p: I completely agree. Even if you've never been near a ceremony like that, I think what she described is extremely relatable. "If you just stop thinking that way. If you just stop feeling that way. If you just change your behaviors." Okay, but how? How do we do that without rejecting who we are and how we feel? Compassionately noticing, normalizing, and even permitting how we feel is necessary for the process of self-regulation. So "just think differently, feel differently, act differently" is a nice idea, but it's also kind of ridiculous.
Here's what she does instead:

q: The first step is to notice. Then, sit with it for a bit and notice what is happening, which is usually the lack of what can be noticed, but this is important. So I get to the point of, oh, here I am in shutdown, and I'm grateful I've seen this. Then, I make a list of what I can do to start the process of shifting. Journaling, somatic practice to be in my body, maybe some music and movement, running my hands up and down my arms and or legs, touching my face. Be patient and gentle.

blocks.p: Those are really good ideas, and they're awesome because they come from her. It's what her body wants. It's telling her what it needs, and she acts on it. That's perfect. I'd invite you to do the same. I don't know if running your hands up and down your arms is right for you. I'm not here to give a prescription, "just do this and you'll feel better." If you can permit yourself to feel the way you feel, your body will tell you what it needs, eventually, if you can listen deeply enough.
One listener wrote: "I didn't know what I didn't know. 70 is late to analyze childhood trauma."

I get what she's saying. Is seventy too late to start working on yourself, on self-regulation, on getting more satisfaction from life? No, obviously not. Is it later than twenty-four? Yes, it's later. But it's not too late. It's a lot better than too late. It's better than seventy-one, or seventy-two, or eighty, or ninety. If you're working on this at seventy, you still have more life to go, and I'm glad you're doing it.

Does that mean you have to delve into childhood trauma? I don't think so. That's not the way I work, and it's not the way I teach. If you want to, go ahead. But right now, in the present moment, you can put some attention, some compassion, some mindfulness into what you feel. Can we connect with the experience of numbness in this moment? Yes, we can do that. Do we have to reflect on childhood trauma in this moment? No.

I think a lot more good can come from prioritizing feeling safe, and then permitting the other feelings to be there, the ones we typically try to avoid, than from trying to address specific instances of childhood trauma. And that's not just for seventy-year-olds. That's for everybody. If you keep building safety and then feel ready to address childhood trauma, or other traumas, a week from now, months or years from now, sure, go right ahead. But in this present moment, it's not too late to add a little more safety to your life, or compassion toward the stuff that doesn't feel great. Honestly, it's the present moment, so it's probably the perfect time.

blocks.h: The sun is above the clouds

blocks.p: One listener, in shutdown within the past year, wrote:

q: The sun is always above the clouds. If you do not see the sun or feel its warmth, it does not mean it is not there. Shutdown alters your perception of reality. What you feel is real is not reality.

blocks.p: That's really interesting, and it's correct: whatever state we're in filters our experience of reality. There is an objective reality outside of us, and the state we're in, whether it's safety, flight, fight, shutdown, freeze, or something else, becomes a filter on it. Someone in shutdown experiences things differently than someone in fight. Neither is right or wrong. It's different.

Someone in safety probably has a more present-moment, objective connection with external reality. Does that mean they're always right? Of course not. But their present-moment connection is stronger than someone in a defensive state. As you access more and more safety, you'll notice how fundamentally different reality is: how much more enlivened you are within, and how much more vibrant the world is outside.
The metaphor of the sun above the clouds is so perfect for shutdown, too. As self-regulation unfolds, the clouds clear, and then we can see the sun. We can touch safety.

Shutdown feels alone, and it kind of is alone. But you're not alone in the sense that there are absolutely other people going through what you're going through. What struck me most in this survey was all the positivity, all the love, that people in shutdown had to give, even to strangers.
One listener wrote a long letter to you:

q: Hi Friend, I'm here. May my own experiences of shutdown offer you a sense that you are truly not alone. We may have not experienced shutdown together in the exact same time or the exact same ways, but I know that it is that experience of being so immobile we can't move, barely move, or want to move, or make a sound, or make the tiniest single efforts, or anything at all. You still love who you love, you still love the things you love, you are still you. That hasn't changed because of your shutdown.

It's an honestly uncomfortable thing when you just don't want to do a single thing, and I get it. There are truly so many real reasons for your shutdown. Real experiences of times when you were being a genuine human being, trying to survive those moments. Maybe it was during a time when you gave it your all because you cared. Or maybe it was during a time when you thought or felt you were doing the right thing. Or maybe it was people being cruel or releasing their past traumas onto you. Or it was a horrible, frightening event.

Being in shutdown is not a forever thing. It will happen for the time being to help you save what's left of your energy. It's your body watching out for you. It's honestly you being as gentle to yourself as it knows how after what you've went through. So, Friend, you aren't a bad person. You're no word that describes anything remotely bad or negative or unworthy of kindness in any way. You are a human trying to save yourself in one of the most incredible responses we are meant to do.

And just from my own experience, sometimes I am able to climb out of shutdown, like in a force myself to do it kind of way, because you know, life and all the responsibilities. Where sometimes I climb out of shutdown very, very, extremely slowly. And there are times when I have been in shutdown for years. There isn't one clear answer of how to solve it or get out of it. If any of these words feel safe, please take whatever you feel is right for you. Patience, love, rest. Take as much time as you need. Reach out to someone you trust or seek help when you feel ready. Let the world be while you let yourself be. And that is totally okay.

blocks.p: That was incredible. I have nothing to add to it.
A few more, in their own words:

q: Your shutdown experience does not define you. You are very capable of getting out of that state. You're so loved and appreciated. You're so resilient for getting through this.
I feel you. It is going to be okay. Yes, it sucks, but hell, let's keep going and figure or not figure this out together.

blocks.p: I love that message of togetherness, and there's even a little fight activation in it. "Yeah, it sucks, but what the heck, let's do it." There's some motivation there.

q: Even if it completely feels like you are all alone, you are not. Please, please do not give up. Please be extremely kind to yourself. This is part of the human experience. I know it is so tough. Please do not make it harder for yourself.

This too will pass. But you must be curious to understand yourself and show self compassion. Digging in harder doesn't give you the path out of this. Your body is not the enemy and your mind is not the boss. You must connect the two and be curious to know who you are and believe you can heal with authentic connection in time.

blocks.p: That is very wise.

q: Be patient with yourself and don't be afraid to ask for help.

blocks.p: And if asking for help is too much, maybe listening to trusted sources is the first step toward it. If you can do that, is there someone in your life, or a professional, you can ask for help in a way that feels comfortable for you?

blocks.h: They showed up with what they had

blocks.p: Many people told me they got a lot out of doing the survey itself: thinking about this stuff, reflecting on their life, and taking the time to respond knowing it would be shared. They were grateful for the chance to reflect, and grateful for the chance to give to someone else. For someone in shutdown to do that is pretty amazing.

A couple of people started the survey, answered questions, and by the end wrote something like, "I don't have the energy for this anymore. I'm done." Someone on the outside, without our language and our understanding of the Polyvagal Theory, might say that person is lazy. I see this person. They showed up. They started it. They answered the questions. It's not that they didn't want to. They just didn't have the energy to reflect further, or maybe to keep extending compassion to other people. That's kind of sad, but it is what it is. I'm so grateful they showed up and gave the energy they could. And we have what they gave us.

I hope these words help you feel more normal, more validated, and more seen, even though they're from strangers. I hope they help you feel connected to other people who know what you're going through.
